response.title: A Garden's Water Record
response.passage: At West Gate High, the science club began collecting notes about a neighborhood garden after a month with little rain. Their first task was to observe when each plot needed water, rather than guess from the dry soil on the surface. The gardeners cooperated by sharing a notebook, although they disagreed about whether young plants should be watered every day. A reliable pattern appeared only after the students compared notes from several warm and cool days. The group found that the shallow reservoir behind the school was lower than usual, which meant a shortage could become serious if the dry spell continued. Instead of asking everyone to stop watering, the club suggested that each family reserve a bucket of rainwater when possible and water plants early. Some residents welcomed the plan; others worried that it asked too much of families with little time. The students listened to that concern and changed the chart so that recording water use took less than a minute. By the end of the month, more families were using the chart, but the reservoir level had not yet recovered. The club therefore described its result carefully: the project improved how people shared water, but it had not proved that neighborhood use was lower. For the next dry season, the students plan to compare the same months across two years before making a larger claim.
removals: Their first task was to observe when each plot needed water, rather than guess from the dry soil on the surface.
A reliable pattern appeared only after the students compared notes from several warm and cool days.
Some residents welcomed the plan; others worried that it asked too much of families with little time.
The club therefore described its result carefully: the project improved how people shared water, but it had not proved that neighborhood use was lower.
response.extraOption: The school greenhouse closed each afternoon when the last science class ended.

response.title: Two Visits to the River
response.passage: Each spring, students at Brookside High record the current water level in a small river behind the gym. During one morning walk, Ana noticed that a fallen branch divided the flow into two paths. Leaves on the wider side traveled faster, while those near the bank barely moved. Her teacher explained that a river current can change from one place to another, even on the same day. The class returned after lunch and found that recent rain had raised the water level. Because the branch was still there, the students could compare how the same obstacle affected stronger water. Their notes showed that the main current had pushed leaves past the second marker in less time. The class added both visits to its chart instead of treating the first result as a permanent pattern. The teacher said repeated observations helped them describe conditions without claiming that every river behaves the same way.
